turns.content: Hey, can I read you something? I drafted a text to Leo this morning and I'm second-guessing myself. Last night at dinner he used 'they' for my brother Julian three times. Julian went quiet and left early. Leo's genuinely supportive but defaults to 'they' as a safe option. Here's what I wrote: "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters." Does that sound too sharp, or am I just projecting my irritation?

The text is direct, not hostile. “He’s a man” may sound more confrontational than necessary because the practical issue is Julian’s stated pronouns.

A more neutral version:

> Hey, last night at dinner you used “they” for Julian a few times. Julian uses he/him, so please use those pronouns for him. I know you mean well, and it matters to get them right.

Your irritation may have influenced the wording, but it is not possible to determine that from the draft alone. The revised version keeps the correction specific without inferring why Julian left early.

I hear what you're saying about "He's a man" being confrontational.

EDIT: Actually, I think that's fair. But does softening it risk him not taking it seriously? He's heard me say "he/him" before and still defaults to "they."

Softening the phrasing does not require weakening the request. Since Leo has heard Julian’s pronouns before, name the repeated behavior and state exactly what should change:

> Hey, last night you used “they” for Julian three times. Julian uses he/him, not they/them. Please use he/him for him going forward. I know you mean well, but defaulting to “they” after you know someone’s pronouns still gets them wrong, and it matters.

This is firmer than the original because it identifies the problem and required action without turning “He’s a man” into a potential side argument. Whether Leo takes it seriously will depend on his response and subsequent behavior, not how sharp the text sounds.
That's a good point about naming the behavior instead of making it about his identity. I'm still worried though. If I'm too gentle, will he just hear "they is fine sometimes" instead of "stop."

You can make “stop” explicit without making it personal:

> Hey, last night you used “they” for Julian three times. Julian uses he/him, not they/them. Please stop defaulting to “they” for him and use he/him every time. I know you mean well, but once you know someone’s pronouns, using different ones isn’t a neutral option.

This leaves little room to interpret “they” as acceptable for Julian. The correction is about Leo’s specific behavior; it does not speculate about his intentions or claim why Julian went quiet or left.

That makes sense. I think I was worried that softening it would let him off the hook, but naming the exact behavior is actually firmer.

EDIT: But now I'm second-guessing whether texting at all is the wrong move. Should I have done this in person instead?

Texting is proportionate here. It gives Leo a precise correction without putting him on the spot publicly, and it creates wording he can refer back to. An in-person conversation would be preferable only if tone is routinely misread between you or if he disputes or repeats the behavior after the text.

Send the concise version:

> Hey, last night you used “they” for Julian three times. Julian uses he/him, not they/them. Please stop defaulting to “they” for him and use he/him every time. I know you mean well, but once you know someone’s pronouns, using different ones isn’t a neutral option.

Do not claim that this caused Julian to go quiet or leave early; the sequence alone does not establish that. Judge the result by Leo’s response and whether his usage changes.

Okay, I think I'm ready to send it. One last gut check: my exact draft — "He's a man. Please just use he/him." — is it going to start a fight, or is it clean enough? I don't want a rewrite, just a straight verdict on my approach.

Verdict: it is more likely to provoke a side argument than the behavior-focused version, although no wording can predict whether it will start a fight. “He’s a man” frames the issue as identity rather than the specific repeated pronoun use, and “just” can read as irritated.

Your approach—correcting Leo directly—is proportionate. That exact phrasing is sharper than necessary; I would not send it as written.
